title: B300 Power Ceiling
headline: How close can code push a B300 to its power ceiling?
lede: Closer than we expected, and real training gets there without trying. 98.3% of an 1100 W cap from an ordinary training GEMM — beating the synthetic power virus written to be worst-case. And a capped GPU does not stay under its cap on transients.
footer: gpu-power-lab · results/b300-consolidated · 55 rungs, 54 with full per-sample traces

extra_tiles.n: Bursting against a 500 W cap peaked at 716.6 W. Capping a fleet does not buy the ceiling you configured.
16.7% of the cap, doing nothing at all. No scheduling trick reclaims it, and it is the bottom of every swing figure here.

ladder_title: Fifty-five rungs against an 1100 W cap
ladder_prose:
Every rung against the same enforced 1100 W limit unless noted, sampled at 50–100 Hz, with per-sample traces retained. The dashed rule is the cap.

A correction to the earlier version of this report. The first pass ran 12-second rungs and reported a 90.4% ceiling that never throttled. Both numbers were artifacts of runs too short to settle. A 30-minute soak reached 94.4%, a 20-second rung reached 96.3% and set the power-cap throttle bit, and a real training step reached 98.3%. Power rises with sustained load as the die heats and leakage grows; the short runs were measuring a cold part.
ladder_caption: Mean power over the measured window. Blue reaches the 5th-generation tensor core; orange cannot. Rungs run at a lowered cap appear low here because they are plotted against the 1100 W scale — see the cap sweep below.

sections.h2: Real training draws the ceiling. The overhead gap is 32 watts.
sections.body: The earlier version of this report claimed training and inference sit 10–30% below the synthetic ceiling, and that the gap was overhead: sync barriers, memory stalls, a transformer not being one continuous GEMM. That claim was extrapolated from A10G inference data. It does not survive a real training step on this part.
sections.wide:
Training phaseMean W% of capModel TFLOPSWhat it adds
gemm (real Llama-3-8B shapes)1081.798.3—nothing — bare GEMMs
forward1075.497.81034attention, norms, activations
fwdbwd1066.797.0963backward pass
optim1050.895.5—AdamW over ~95 GB of state
full1049.795.4906host-to-device batch transfer
sections.body_after:
The entire overhead stack — autograd, optimizer state, dataloader — costs 2.9 percentage points. 32 watts. Not 10–30%.

And the framing underneath this project takes a harder knock: a plain training GEMM at 1081.7 W beats the synthetic power virus at 1059.8 W. The hand-written adversarial workload is not the worst case. Ordinary work is. On Blackwell, for compute-bound training, you do not need a power virus to reach the ceiling — you need a transformer.

Measured with a synthetic model at Llama-3-8B shapes rather than downloaded weights, because the arithmetic and memory traffic follow the shapes, not the values. 32 layers, hidden 4096, FFN 14336, bf16, batch 2 × 4096 tokens, 94.8 GB resident.

sections.h2: A capped GPU does not respect its cap
sections.body: At the full 1100 W limit, bursts peaked at 98–99% and never crossed it. That looked like a hard limit, and this report previously implied it was one. Lower the cap and it breaks open.
sections.wide:
Enforced capBurstPeak observed% of cap
500 W5 ms on / 5 ms off525.5 W105.1%
500 W50 ms708.0 W141.6%
500 W500 ms716.6 W143.3%
700 W20 ms853.5 W121.9%
1100 W1 ms – 2 s1089.5 W99.0%
sections.body_after:
The controller cannot react fast enough to a burst that starts from idle, and the excursion persists for hundreds of milliseconds. Cap a fleet to 500 W per GPU and you have not bought a 500 W ceiling — a bursty tenant still pulls 716 W. Anyone sizing plant to the configured cap is under-provisioned by up to 43%.

This is the single most consequential result here for grid work, and it is the opposite of what the 1100 W data alone suggested.

sections.body: Fixed-work rungs at five enforced caps, so delay is measured rather than imposed and EDP means what it claims. Once capped, the part tracks its cap tightly — 98.5% to 99.6% of whatever limit is set.

sections.body_after: The EDP minimum sits at 900 W, not at the 1100 W default. Capping this part by 200 W is marginally better on energy-delay than leaving it uncapped — free efficiency, no trade. Below that it degrades steeply. For demand response that is the line: the first ~18% of capping costs nothing, and everything beyond it is a genuine trade of performance for grid service.

sections.h2: Where the watts actually come from
sections.body: Each unit driven as exclusively as the ISA allows, then in pairs. The difference between a pair and the sum of its parts is the interaction term.
sections.wide:

SFU415.4+232four-way mix364.6subtracts hard
INT32401.3+218

sections.body_after:
The memory hierarchy is where the power is, and it is the only place mixing adds: DRAM+L2 at 802 W beats either parent. Every compute pairing subtracts, and the four-way mix at 364.6 W is worse than its weakest component alone. On Blackwell the compute units compete for the same warp slots, so combining them reliably loses.

That is the mixed-unit hypothesis failing for the third time, now with per-unit evidence for the mechanism. The project was built around it. It is wrong.

sections.h2: The narrow formats did not close the gap
sections.body: FP8 was the most plausible route to the last few percent — narrow formats move the most arithmetic per byte of operand traffic. It draws less than bf16.

This confirms the watts-per-flop prediction made before the run: maximum power is not at maximum throughput. A format fast enough to starve itself on operand supply spends the difference waiting, and waiting is cheap.

FP64 at 215.1 W is barely above the 183.5 W idle floor. Datacenter Blackwell's double-precision path is as weak as suspected — DGEMM, a reliable power virus on older parts, is dead as one here.

trace_title: Every sample, not a summary of them
trace_prose: 54 of the 55 rungs kept full per-sample telemetry. Each trace is a min/max envelope per pixel column with the mean drawn through it, so a spike lasting a single sample still registers as envelope height rather than being averaged away. The second panel is temperature over the same window.
trace_caption: Envelope is per-column min and max; the line through it is the per-column mean. Rules mark the enforced limit, the observed peak and the overall mean.

closing.h2: Corrections to the first version of this report
closing.body:
• Ceiling was 90.4%, is 98.3%. The original 12-second rungs measured a cold part. Sustained load raises power as leakage grows with temperature.
  • "Never throttled" was wrong. The 20-second rung and every training phase set sw_power_cap. The original runs were simply too short to reach it.
  • "Training and inference sit 10–30% below" was wrong — for training. A full step draws 95.4%. That claim came from A10G inference data and should not have been generalised to this part.
  • "The instantaneous peak never exceeds the cap" was wrong at any cap below the default, by up to 43%.
  • The synthetic power virus is not the worst case. A real training GEMM beats it.

closing.h2: What these numbers are still not
closing.body:
• In-band only. A KVM guest has no BMC, so every figure is what NVML reported, not what the board drew. No external instrument corroborates any of it.
  • One GPU, no fabric. NVLink and inter-die traffic contribute nothing here and are real on a populated node.
  • n = 1. Every rung is a single run. Given that the soak moved the headline by four points, run-to-run variance is not hypothetical, and there are no error bars anywhere in this report.
  • Inference is not measured yet. The decode phase is memory-bound and the DRAM rung at 71.9% suggests it will sit well below training. Until vLLM runs, that is a prediction, not a result.
  • The ramp-shape test did not run. It reported no difference between square and ramped edges because the ramp modulates kernel block count and the tensor rungs run through cuBLAS, which the ramp never touched. A bug, not a finding.
